claim: The CAS follow-ups define four mechanisms: a mechanism-agnostic skipped-transaction detector, per-phase rows in `system.content_addressed_garbage_collection_log`, an `S42` verdict based on consistency assertions, and an opt-in mount-time force-claim.
The skipped-transaction detector must detect the effect that a fold cursor advanced past a ref-log transaction that was never applied, rather than assume that the cause was a hole in a `LIST` page.

A publish appends both `precommitAdd` and `promote` ref-log transactions; `precommitAdd` carries the activation `+1` edge, while `promote` moves the owner at the same `manifest_ref` and emits no edge.

The raw `dropRefTransition` and `publishCommittedTransition` test helpers must not be mixed with the real writer on one namespace because the helpers allocate sequences by listing while the writer uses an in-memory sequence, causing collisions when the namespace is written again.

A `HoleyListBackend` test must arm `omitFromNthListCall` after all seeding writes because writer-side namespace listing for sequence allocation consumes qualifying `LIST` calls and otherwise shifts the selected call.

`HoleyListBackend` omits one chosen durable key from one qualifying `list` call while leaving exact `get` and `head` for that key functional, modeling an incomplete enumeration without modeling a particular pagination mechanism.

A GC round enumerates the `cas/refs/` prefix twice: `Gc::preFoldRefScan` supplies the defer signal and `Gc::fold` performs the folding walk; only a hole in the fold walk reproduces the skipped-transaction defect.

In the retention direction, omitting a ref-log removal record can advance the cursor past that record permanently, so the removal is never folded and the residual activation edge retains the blob after the listing recovers.

In the deletion direction, omitting a second live owner's activation `+1` while folding the first owner's removal can make GC compute zero in-degree for a blob still referenced by a committed manifest and delete that blob.
The `BlobDelta` row remains 64 bytes when `txn_ordinal` is placed after `remove`, because the ordinal occupies existing tail padding; `kBlobDeltaSize` and a `static_assert` pin this hot-path size.

`BlobDelta::txn_ordinal` must remain the last member unless positional aggregate initializers are converted, because inserting it before `remove` silently rebinds `BlobDelta{ref, source_id, remove}` and turns removals into activations.

Ref transaction identifiers are allowed to have safe gaps: an append refused before any network attempt can leave a gap, so a missing id in an otherwise ordered sequence is not by itself evidence of incomplete enumeration.
Probe A compares the two existing full enumerations of `cas/refs/` instead of performing another scan, so it adds a set comparison and no backend I/O.

Probe A reports a disagreement only when a ref-log id is present in one enumeration, absent from the other, and strictly below the other enumeration's maximum id for the same namespace; this witness condition excludes normal concurrent appends.

Probe A cannot detect a hole reproduced identically in both enumerations or a namespace omitted wholesale from one enumeration, and widening the rule to use the pre-scan maximum as a witness was rejected because it can permanently block legitimate cleanup.

When Probe A detects a disagreement, ref folding is aborted for the round: cursors do not advance, accumulated deltas are discarded, parent cursors are carried into the seal, and destructive actions are suppressed.

Probe B1 compares a running count of logs applied at the single `resolved_through = log_id` cursor-advance site with a seal-time recomputation from sealed coverage and the ref listing; it is a control-flow assertion and is blind to a record missing from that same listing.
`TxnApplyLedger` is round-local and never persisted; it tracks each opened ref transaction, whether it produced deltas, whether intake committed it, and whether a reducer consumed at least one delta.

Probe B2 marks a transaction applied at reducer consumption rather than run flush, because the in-degree model is a set and legitimate unmatched removals or duplicate activations may disappear during set merging.

A committed transaction that produced blob deltas but whose deltas reached no shard reducer causes the GC round to throw `CORRUPTED_DATA` before the seal write, adopt nothing, reclaim nothing, and direct recovery through `SYSTEM CONTENT ADDRESSED GC REBUILD`.

`GcRoundLogRecord` uses a fresh `round_id` for every round attempt and stamps it on Start, Phase, and Finish rows; `round` is unsuitable because it is zero on Start, unavailable on non-leader rounds, and known only after a folding CAS.
The garbage-collection log phase schema adds `EventType::Phase`, `round_id`, `phase`, `phase_duration_us`, and `phase_metrics` without removing or reordering existing fields.

`meta_pool_wait` must report explicit `jobs_scheduled` and `jobs_completed` metrics because work scheduled on the meta pool runs on other threads and is absent from the fold thread's `ProfileEvents` delta.
Phase timing is always enabled with no setting; `GcPhaseTimer` uses a snapshot difference of the current thread's `ProfileEvents` rather than a nested `ProfileEventsScope`.

The `S42` verdict treats a consistent on-disk and in-memory state as the deciding result; targeted post-durable-install counters are reported rather than gating, while the generic anti-vacuity guard remains gating.
`Verdict.reported` records a genuinely non-gating observation without affecting run status, and must not be used to soften an assertion or convert unavailable data into a pass.

Force-claiming by overwriting the owner uuid permanently locks the original server out, whereas adopting the pool's existing owner uuid via `Pool::openForDecommission` reaches a WRITE mount without durable identity damage; the choice remains a user decision.

`ForeignMountDeath` classifies a foreign mount slot as `Absent`, `CleanFarewell`, `GcFenced`, `ObservedStable`, or `Live`; only the first four provide a certificate usable by the opt-in force-claim path.

`proveForeignMountDead` never treats `expires_at_ms <= now_ms` alone as proof of death; absent, farewell, and GC-fenced slots decide immediately, while other slots require an unchanged write token across `mountObservationThresholdMs(ttl_ms, poll_interval_ms)` on the observer's monotonic clock.

The force-claim write order is read-only death proof, token-conditional owner overwrite, unchanged `allocateWriterEpoch`, exact-token deletion of the stale mount slot, and then ordinary `claimMount`; deleting the slot before epoch allocation would disarm the guard against re-minting `writer_epoch 1`.
`force_owner_claim` is an opt-in per-disk setting that permits a writable open with a differing configured server uuid to claim the server-root as WRITE only after a mount-slot death certificate.
The ordinary `claimMount` invariant remains unchanged: a different `server_uuid` is `ForeignOwner` and must not be written over, regardless of expiry or prior state.

The force-claim CI motivation was removed by a one-line configuration-scrape fix, while force-claim remains a separate operator need; the relevant CI scrape runs after server termination and the force-claim tasks were intentionally left unstarted.
A diagnostic CAS reader that does not claim ownership must not schedule GC or mint writer state, and read-only enforcement should be below facade checks at the CAS `Backend` layer.
The mount claim protects writer identity, writer epochs, live double starts, the local write fence, and the mount's in-flight builds from GC; it does not provide a stable reader view.

A mounted `Pool` caches `RefTableState` and does not re-recover it, while `CasFsck.cpp` deliberately uses a fresh `recoverRefTable`; a non-claiming read can therefore be less stale on the ref lane than a mounted read.

A non-claiming read-only pool has an unarmed local write fence, so the current read-only guarantee depends on seven `checkNotReadOnly` facade checks and on not starting the GC scheduler; the CAS `Backend` interface itself has no read-only concept.

A non-claiming reader has exactly one identified wrong-answer class: a superseded GC generation can disappear mid-scan, causing `openSourceEdgeRun` to throw `CORRUPTED_DATA` on a healthy pool; this is independent of mount ownership.

For other concurrent-read observations, CAS fsck is designed to fail closed or report an inconclusive result: fresh reference checks treat a concurrently deleted blob or manifest as still referenced, checksum failures are catalogued as `CorruptedRun`, and timeouts set `partial=1`.

Letting tools claim ownership and downgrading failures afterward is rejected because a tool can claim a fresh empty pool under uuid `0000…`, burn a durable writer epoch before refusal, and join the GC heartbeat ack floor.

The recommended reader contract is observe-only by process role: a CA disk opened by a non-`SERVER` application never claims the mount, mints writer state, or schedules GC, while writable tool access requires an explicit opt-in.

A fail-closed read-only `Backend` decorator should make every `put*` and `delete*` operation throw `READONLY`; `ca-gc-rebuild`'s single `gc/state` CAS must be an explicit exception rather than an accidental hole.

The CI scrape was post-mortem rather than concurrent: `ClickHouseProc.dump_system_tables` stops the server before using `clickhouse local`, and the CA pool is opened under an unrelated identity against the same data directory.

The CI scrape is conditional on a failed functional-test result, and the stop operation is best-effort; therefore a force-claim liveness guard must be real even though the normal scrape is post-mortem.

Forcing only the owner anchor cannot mount a foreign pool because the mount slot retains the predecessor's `server_uuid` and ordinary `claimMount` rejects it as `ForeignOwner`; a graceful shutdown leaves that slot with `min_active == UINT64_MAX` rather than deleting it.
The force-claim surface is `<force_owner_claim>true</force_owner_claim>` as a per-disk setting, defaulting to false and carried into `Cas::PoolConfig::force_owner_claim`.
`proveForeignMountDead` returns `Live` when a foreign holder's token keeps changing across the bounded observation restarts; the force path must throw `ABORTED` and write nothing in that case.

Force-claim preserves the durable monotone writer epoch by running `allocateWriterEpoch` before deleting the stale mount slot; it then deletes the slot with `deleteExact` using the observed token and invokes unmodified `claimMount`.
A successful force-claim must emit a warning and a `CasEvent` audit record naming the displaced uuid, the new uuid, and the death certificate used.

A force-claim permanently reassigns pool identity: the original server presents its old uuid on restart and is refused by `claimOwnerOrThrow` until the owner object is restored or `server_root_id` is reconfigured.

`Pool::openForDecommission` already provides a reversible alternative by reading the existing owner uuid and impersonating it, preserving pool identity while allowing a WRITE mount; its tradeoff is that two processes present the same owner uuid and rely on the mount lease to serialize them.
The ref-log cursor is sealed above every record a GC round observed, not every record that exists; an omitted durable ref log can therefore never be folded by a later incremental round.

The observed CAS ref-prefix enumeration omitted two objects that had been durable for nineteen seconds while returning a third object written 2.2 milliseconds after them; the store-side mechanism remains unknown.

The captured disagreement involved namespace `ca_soak_ch1/store/3ba/3ba2c30d-d1b2-4b17-a536-d311f1e239d4@cas@`, missing ref transactions `epoch 1, seq 0x1430c` and `epoch 1, seq 0x1430d`, and pre-fold maximum `epoch 1, seq 0x1430e`.

The observed hole firing was not explained by a phantom key, concurrent ref-object deletion, stale-epoch minting, out-of-order appends, late landing, page-limit mismatch, or different key filters: the hole keys were `HEAD`-present, there were zero ref-object deletes in the relevant minute, all 65,263 uploads were ordered by writer epoch, and both walks used limit 1000 and `parseRefObjectKey`.
When Probe A fired, the round aborted folding, held the cursor, and a later complete enumeration folded the missing records; the three keys were deleted six minutes later and no leak resulted.

Historical and live holes form short adjacent runs rather than dropped pages: one historical firing had 13 holes across two namespaces, and the live capture had two adjacent holes immediately below the witness id `0x1430e`.

Across historical firings, 338,559 objects were missing from the fold scan and 58 were missing from the pre-fold scan; only the latter direction is not explained by concurrent deletion because the fold scan demonstrably saw the objects.

The direct listing hammer did not reproduce holes in about 19 million listed keys, but it did not reproduce the real CAS conditions: it used boto3 against a healthy store, lacked the ClickHouse S3 client's retries and chaos, and used different concurrency and key shape.

A failed diagnostic command must not be converted to a confident zero with `|| echo 0`; permission denied, a missing file, and no match are distinct outcomes, and container logs should be read with `docker exec` when host permissions deny access.

At firing time, `HEAD` distinguishes the two opposite enumeration defects: `present` means a durable object was omitted by an enumeration, while `absent` means the other enumeration returned a nonexistent key and indicts the client or iterator; this distinction cannot be recovered after legitimate deletion.

A `gc_anomaly` audit record carries the probe, ref transaction id, missing direction, `HEAD` verdict, both enumeration maxima, hole ordinal, row cap, namespace, and `outcome = ref_folding_aborted`; a bare anomaly count is insufficient forensic context.

Counters such as `CasGcProbeAHolePresent` and `CasGcProbeAHoleAbsent` are process-local and can be erased by chaos restarts, whereas `gc_anomaly` audit rows survive; both carriers are needed for field diagnosis.

The in-degree reducer models source edges as a set: an unmatched `-1` is dropped as a no-op and a duplicate `+1` collapses, so the reducer must not materialize negative edges merely to repair the retention leak.

A residual `+1` can arise either because its `-1` ref-log was omitted and the cursor sealed past it, or because the `-1` reached the reducer before its `+1`; the latter is counted by `CasGcUnmatchedRemoveDeltas` and is a separate investigation.

Measured GC performance found `fold_ref_intake` linear in the ref-log backlog at 256 logs/s, with round trips equal to `logs + 2 × edges`; 39.6% of intake manifest fetches were cross-transaction re-reads, making a round-scoped body cache a potential optimization.
One observed `pending_deletes` phase lasted 77.2 seconds, compared with 243 milliseconds for the next-worst phase, making it a significant uninvestigated performance cost.

The durable fix requirement is that GC must not advance a cursor over records whose enumeration it cannot prove complete; the committed direction is an authoritative per-namespace chain plus a complete-cut gate.

The fix must not assume holes are page-shaped or trust a particular store, must retain Probe A and its `HEAD` verdict, and should close Probe A's two blind spots with the authoritative chain rather than widen its witness rule.
